series: Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs, Section 2: Finance and Risk
title: Make Clean Power an Asset Class

slides.title: Make Clean Power an Asset Class
slides.subtitle: Standardized de-risking for developing countries: Briefs 2.1 and 2.2
slides.message: Clean power is cheap to build and dear to finance, because investors price risks the plant cannot control. Remove payment risk at its source, then turn projects into a few standard securities. Standardization, not subsidy, lowers the price.

slides.title: Capital, not technology, prices clean power

stats.label: cost of the same solar plant at 12% cost of capital (6.5 c/kWh) against 4% (3.6 c/kWh)
solar cost of capital in key emerging economies, against advanced ones and China (2021)
of the cost of solar was financing in developing economies, against 25–30% in advanced ones

slides.text: Panels are bought at world prices. What differs is the risk investors price around the plant, and almost none of it is the plant's own. Costs exclude construction interest: 5.7 c/kWh at 10%, or 6.2 c/kWh with two years of it (Brief 2.2).

slides.title: The risk stack, and who should hold each layer
rows: An intermediary that can wait for arrears and recover them
Payment intermediary with a guarantee waterfall
Banks and DFIs that can supervise it
Construction loans against a contingent PPA
Senior synthetic sovereign bonds on pooled plants
First-loss tranche held by a regional fund
Local-currency senior tranche; a denomination rule
Nobody: it can be priced and conditioned, not transferred
Guarantees conditional on utility and tariff reform
slides.note: Single instruments disappoint because they treat a stack of separable risks as one.

slides.title: Payment risk first: the intermediary
slides.caption: Expected value per year by layer, stylized 2 GW regional facility, $ million.
points: One standard PPA; generators paid in full and on time whatever the distributor does.
Arrears become a debt to a repeat creditor that can wait and recover.
Layers agreed before the first tender: offtaker, state owner, national intercept, multilateral agency, donor account.
A $57m buffer bridges 99.5th-percentile arrears on $174m a year of contracts.

slides.title: Guarantee the contract, not the debt

stats.label: a year saved by the buyer under a contract guarantee, for $0.18m of expected cost
a year saved under a debt guarantee, for $0.40m of expected cost
tariff saving per dollar of expected cost, contract against debt guarantee

slides.text: Stylized 100 MW plant: tariff 5.50 c/kWh unguaranteed, 4.96 with a contract guarantee, 5.33 with a debt guarantee. The contract guarantor's worst case is $8.7m a year of arrears; the debt guarantor's is $60m of debt. (This 5.3 is not series 3's sovereign guarantee multiplier: about 80 on the MDB loss record, 2.7 in its stress case.)

slides.title: What India's SECI shows, good and bad

left.heading: What works
points: Rated AAA: about 60 GW sold at Rs 2.93/kWh on a 7-paise margin, 2.4% of the tariff.
Letters of credit enforced through grid scheduling since 2019; a payment security fund.
Tripartite agreement: the RBI can debit a defaulting state's account; invoked in 2020–22.

right.heading: What it did not fix
points: Letter-of-credit coverage only 68%; large past delays.
Rs 90,000 crore liquidity scheme (2020); arrears rescheduled into up to 48 installments (2022).
Legacy arrears fell from Rs 1,39,947 crore to Rs 3,330 crore by March 2026: risk moved to the center, not removed.

slides.text: Nigeria's bulk trader shows the failure case: a single buyer with no reliable revenue behind it. Only utility reform reduces the risk.

slides.title: Split at commissioning, pool and tranche
slides.caption: Cost of power from the stylized plant, US c/kWh, with two years of construction interest.
points: Banks and DFIs build against a contingent PPA: a creditworthy buyer waiting.
Operating plants are pooled across countries under one contract.
Three securities: first-loss equity, a thin mezzanine, a senior synthetic sovereign bond.
Pooled at 5.65%: 4.6 c/kWh against 6.2, 27% less.

slides.title: Subordination and pooling: the results

stats.label: subordination for a near-AAA senior bond at correlation 0.10; 7.7% at 0.20
needed by a ten-country pool, against 9.2% for one country
of the pool funded by the senior bond (correlation 0.20)
expected cost over ten years of guaranteeing a $460m mezzanine

slides.text: Correlation, not the default rate, drives the cushion, and the host sovereign is its main source. With twice the defaults and 72% recovery, power still costs 4.7 c/kWh. The mezzanine guarantee is cheap in expectation but can be fully drawn in a crisis.

slides.title: How the pieces compose; what the host owes

left.heading: A project's life
points: An intermediary makes offtake contracts bankable.
A contingent contract lets the developer borrow to build at a market rate.
The finished plant is pooled and refinanced through a synthetic sovereign bond.
Conditions on guarantees improve the utilities that caused the problem.

right.heading: The host's contingent liability
points: The state stands in the waterfall and in the second tier of grid guarantees.
Expected national calls: about 2% of contract payments in a 2 GW facility.
Smaller, contingent and contracted, but not zero: record it at expected cost, cap it, report it.

slides.text: Each piece is weaker alone. Section 3's guarantee capacity can stand in the waterfall; the Trust's regional funds can hold first loss.

slides.title: What to do
todo: Build national or regional payment intermediaries: one PPA, a waterfall signed before the first tender.
Contract in local currency on declining tariffs; make utility reform a condition of entry.
Write a contingent PPA and a published take-out into every auction.
Sponsor regional pools; regional funds hold first loss, highly rated sovereigns guarantee the mezzanine.
Record the host's guarantees at expected cost, under a cap.
